label: paragraph_title
text: MINERS' EXECUTIVE MOVE.

label: paragraph_title
text: Hint of. Climax Being Reached.

label: text
text: The Miners' Executive met this evening to discuss fresh proposals for ending the dispute. At the close of the meeting they proceeded to the House of Commons to confer with the Parliamentary Labour Party Executive.

label: text
text: Sir William Joynson Hicks, Home Secretary, moved a resolution for the continuance of the Emergency Regulations, and his speech was much interrupted from the Labour Benches, one member, Mr. Jack Jones, being suspended after refusing to accept the ruling of the Speaker.

label: text
text: Referring to the business before the House of Commons M. Ramsay MacDonald suggested that instead of proceeding to discuss the general situation in the coal dispute before the discussion on the renewal of the regulations, the general debate should be taken to tomorrow as certain conferences were being held to day and certain explorations were being made regarding the situation.

label: text
text: This course was adopted.

label: text
text: Sir W. Joynson. Hicks said that the chief value of these regulations was in their preventive effect. On the whole the mining disغriets had remained quiet and orderly, and he paid a tribute to the excellent behaviour of the great emission of miners most of whom were suffering under what they considered a great sense of grievance. During last month only 64 cases had been taken under the provisions of the Emergency Regulations; and the bulk of those concerned in such cases were not miners.

label: text
text: Mr. Ramsay MacDonald contended that no case of continuing the regulations had been established. The country was peaceful, and there had been nothing in the history of this or any other country of such a quiet and orderly prosecution of an industrial dispute. The worst that had happened could, he said, be dealt with adequately under the ordinary law.

label: text
text: The debate is proceeding. British Wireless Service.

label: paragraph_title
text: Buldwin's Message.

label: text
text: When the House of Commons reassembled for the special purpose of renewing the Emergency Regulations in connection with the coal dispute Commander J. M. Kenworthy (Liberal Central Hull) asked whether Mr. Baldwin's message to the American newspapers as regards the condition of the miners and their families had been sent through our Ambassador in Washington in consultation with the Foreign Office.

label: text
text: Sir Austen Chamberlain replied that the message was not sent through the Ambassador but, "with my knowledge and full concurrence." (Conservative cheers).

label: text
text: Sir W. Joynson Hicks, in moving the resolution authorising the continuance of the regulations for a month, said that "there had been only 64 prosections. Thereunder in August. Their chief value was preventive. The mining districts generally were quiet and orderly." He would like to pay tribute to the miners--(Labourite interruptions in which Mr. Jack Jones was most prominent).

label: text
text: The Speaker asked Mr. Jones to withdraw.

label: text
text: Mr. Jones began his exit at a snail's piece, stopping at intervals to abuse the Government benches. He was finally suspended by 235 votes to 53.

label: text
text: Sir H. Slesser (Labourite, South-East Leeds) moved to terminate zero of the emergency regulations - one dealing with nets likely to reuse edition and the other with public meetings and processions.

label: text
text:
Sir W. Joynson Hicks said that if the safety men were called out by Mr. Cook or anyone else it would be the duty of the Government to take all possible steps to prevent the mines and the livelihood of the miners being destroyed. (Ministerial cheers). That was an elementary duty, and a duty that would be carried out to the full.
The House renewed the Emergency Regulations for another month by 232 votes to 91 and adjourned till to-morrow the general discussion on the coal situation.
Reuter

label: text
text: The balance at credit of Profit and Loss Account for the year ending May 31, 1926, is $4,678.78, after allowing for necessary depreciation of stocks and making reservation for bad and doubtful debts. With the sum of $4,481.12 brought forward from previous year, there is the sum of $9,159.90 to be dealt with. It is proposed to appropriate $5,000 to write down cost of patent rights, plant, etc. of Metallisation, Ltd. and to carry forward a balance of $4,159.90 to next account.

label: text
text: It is to be regretted that figures do not permit us to recommend a dividend on this occasion, but it is many years since you have had to go without a dividend and I am sure you will agree that it is far better to build up our resources than dig into reserves at the present time.

label: text
text: The accounts call for little comment, except that it may become advisable to dispose of our investments in order to improve our cash position.

label: text
text: Conditions in our line of trading have been deplorable during the whole of the financial period under "review and I think we must consider ourselves lucky to have come out on the right side. Demonstration Soon.

label: text
text:
I referred at our last meeting to the fact that we had secured the patent rights and purchased a plant for a process of spraying different metals, called "Metalisation." I had hoped that the results of working would have been reflected in the present Profit and Loss Account. Unfortunately, we have been faced with many unforeseen circumstances and delay in making a start with this process here has been unavoidable. The plant is now practically ready to start up and we hope to give a demonstration to our engineering friends and any shareholders that are interested. All we shall require after that will be plenty of work.
I now propose the adoption of the report and accounts as presented and when this has been seconded shall be glad to answer any questions to the best of my ability.

label: text
text: Dr. Stacy A. Ransom one of the best known men in Shanghai and certainly one of the oldest residents among the American Community at Shanghai died at 8 o'clock last night (August 26) in the General hospital from Bright's disease at the age of 59 years.

label: text
text: DR. STACY A. RANSOM

label: paragraph_title
text: OBITUARY

label: text
text: Dr. Ransom had Been a sufferer from the disease for some considerable time past, but it was not until last week while on a holiday in Peitain to that the symptoms grew worse necessitating a quick return to Shanghai and an immediate entrance into hospital.

label: text
text: Born in Washington D.C., Dr. Ransom was educated at the University of Georgetown and at the age of 26 graduated in Medicine.

label: text
text: Prior to coming to Shanghai in 1902 Dr. Ransom served with the colours in the Spanish American War.

label: text
text: Immediately on reaching Shanghai Dr. Ransom was appointed Quarantine and Medical Officer to the American Consulate General and since then has been the United States Public Health Officer in Shanghai.

label: text
text: A popular member of all the principal clubs, sporting and social, the late doctor was also well-known and esteemed for his public works the chief of which were President of the Shanghai Medical Society. President of the American Association, Chairman of the Board of the Shanghai General Hospital and member of the Shanghai Municipal Council.

label: text
text: In 1903 Dr. Ransom was appointed second in Command of the Shanghai Volunteer Corps which rank he held at the time of his death, and in 1906 he organised and founded the American Company which he commanded for 14 years and which is to-day one of the foremost companies of the Corps.

label: text
text:
A crack shot with the rifle Dr. Rainsom was for a considerable time, Chairman of the Executive Committee of the Shanghai Rifle Association and helped the local team considerably time and time again in a interport rifle matches.
At one time Dr. Ransom, who was a Shriner, was District Grand Master of the local Masonic Lodge.

label: text
text: Dr. Ransom leaves a wife who is now in Shanghai and one son who is at present serving with the American Infantry having graduated from the West Point Military Academy. To both of the bereaved the sympathy of the community will be extended.—“China Press.”

label: paragraph_title
text: ANIMAL COURTSHIP.

label: paragraph_title
text: PROFESSOR J. HUXLEY'S LECTURE.

label: text
text: London, August 10.—One of the most attractive evening lectures before the British Association for the Advancement of Science was delivered by, Professor Julian Huxley on animal 'courtship in which he asserted that Darwin's theory of sexual selection was essentially right, though wrong in many details. The first actions to which the name of courtship must be given were those of a few crabs and most spiders. The male fiddler crab had a huge claw, weighing possibly as much as the rest of its body, and often brightly coloured in the mating season. when the female passed the males assumed a tiptoe attitude and the big claw was held rigidly aloft. If the female did not notice this gesture, the males hurried after her again and struck a statuesque pose.

label: text
text: One type of hunting spiders offered the female a nice fly neatly wrapped in silk like a bouquet.

label: text
text: Web-spinners, which were almost blind, vibrated a thread in the female web in a special way different from the vibration with which they trapped prey. Otherwise they might be eaten by the female who was much bigger than the male. Sometimes the male was eaten after the act of mating. Times of Ceylon.

label: paragraph_title
text: CATHOLIC CONGRESS

label: text
text: CHICAGO ECLIPSED BY MADRID AND VIENNA.

label: text
text: Rome, August 13.

label: text
text:
While the Eucharistic Congress of Chicago was gigantic in dimension and emblematic of America in its democratic setting and "biggest in the world" spirit for magnificence and pomp, it would be hard to surpass the congress held in Madrid in 1911 and Vienna in 1912.
A special solid silver monstrance, wolching seven hundred pounds, placed on a state carriage laden with roses and jasmin and attended by King Alfonso featured the congress of Madrid. In Vienna, the papal legate, Cardinal Van Rossum rode in the golden carriage of the Empress Maria Teresa, drawn by eight pure white Hungarian steeds, followed by the "Emperor Franz Josef in his state coach with emblazoned outriders, accompanied by the Archduke. Ferdinand and the entire court. Ninety thousand persons participated in the procession.
In the course of the final meeting of the Madrid Congress of 1911, King Alfonso made an important speech in which he recalled the historic claims of Spain as a Catholic country. The King and Queen of Spain got down from their state coach to receive the Eucharistic procession when it reached the portals of the royal palace.

label: text
text: The procession which terminated the Viehna Eucharistic Congress, of 1912 was, especially magnificent. More than 8,000 priests, 2,800 officers of the Austrian army, 3,500 state employees, 92 deputies, 260 bishops and 12 cardinals took part in it.

label: text
text: The first Eucharistic Congress was held at Lille in 1881; the second at Avignon, 1882; the third, Liege, 1883; the fourth, Frieburg, Germany, 1885; the fifth, Toulouse, 1886; the sixth, Paris, 1888; the seventh, Antwerp, 1890; and the eighth at Jerusalem in 1892.

label: text
text: The twentieth congress was held at "Cologne in 1900; the 21st, which was the first to be held on the continent of North America, took place at Montreal in 1910, and on all these three occasions Cardinal Vannutelli was the papal legate.

label: text
text: The 22nd congress was celebrated at Madrid, in 1911, the 23rd at Vienna, 1912, and the 24th and 25th at Malta and Lourdes respectively in the year 1913 and 1914. During the War no Eucharistic congress was held.

label: text
text: In 1922, the first post-war congress was held in Rome. It was inaugurated by the present Pope in the Vatican in the presence of 23 cardinals and some 20,000 persons.
